short: 141 days of offensive, and 57,470 British casualties on the first morning alone.
full:
The offensive had been planned as a joint Anglo-French blow, but the German attack at Verdun in February 1916 left Haig's largely volunteer New Armies to carry most of it. A seven-day bombardment fired over 1.5 million shells, many of them defective, and failed to cut the wire or destroy the deep dugouts the Germans had driven into the chalk ridge. At 7.30am on 1 July the infantry advanced. By nightfall the British Army had taken 57,470 casualties, 19,240 of them dead, the worst day in its history.

The battle went on until 18 November. On 15 September, at Flers-Courcelette, tanks were used in action for the first time, in small numbers and with limited effect. The Allies advanced about six miles for something over a million casualties on all sides. The German army was worn down badly enough that it withdrew to the prepared Hindenburg Line the following spring, but in Britain the Somme became shorthand for industrial slaughter.
